evidence.text: The 2023 Act set up a three-member selection committee: the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.

arguments.reasoning: The panel is the Prime Minister, a Cabinet Minister he nominates, and the Leader of the Opposition, so the government side has two votes of three.
arguments.title: Two of three panel members come from the government

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The Act replaced the arrangement set out in the Anoop Baranwal judgment, under which the Chief Justice of India sat on the panel, with a Cabinet Minister.
Hearing the challenge in July 2026, Justice Dipankar Datta asked: "Election Commissioner has to be an independent person. Should there not be a show of fairness?"

arguments.reasoning: Compared with the court's 2023 arrangement, which put the Chief Justice on the panel, the law swapped the only member from outside the executive and legislature for a minister, so the government can now pick commissioners on its own votes.
arguments.title: The law removed the member from outside government

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The ECI said commissioners were previously appointed by prime ministers, that since 2023 they are appointed under a law for the first time, and that "obviously the new system is better".
The Attorney General and Solicitor General argued the Anoop Baranwal judgment was only an interim arrangement and did not limit Parliament's power under Article 324.

arguments.reasoning: Compared with how commissioners were chosen for decades, by the government alone, the law adds the Leader of the Opposition, so it is not less independent than before; the government argues the court's arrangement was only meant to last until Parliament made a law.
arguments.title: Before 2023 the government chose alone

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: About 65 lakh names were left out of the draft roll published on 1 August 2025; the Supreme Court had the ECI post the deleted names with reasons.
The final roll of 30 September 2025 had about 7.42 crore electors, against about 7.89 crore before the revision, a net drop of about 47 lakh, after 21.53 lakh were added and 3.66 lakh more removed.

arguments.reasoning: The ECI's own draft and final rolls show the scale of removals.
arguments.title: 65 lakh off the draft, 47 lakh fewer at the end

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: Petitioners challenged the requirement that voters absent from the 2002 rolls prove a link to someone on those rolls.
During the hearings the court had the ECI publish the deleted names with reasons and, in September 2025, accept Aadhaar as a 12th document for identity.
ADR's counsel told the court the deletions reflect a systemic problem and cited a person deleted in the draft who applied for inclusion but was not restored.

arguments.reasoning: When tens of lakhs are removed and people missing from the 2002 roll must prove links to it, some eligible voters are likely to fall out; the court itself had to add safeguards along the way.
arguments.title: The scale and the paperwork put eligible voters at risk

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed; the checker found the reasoning overreached, so it was reworded to its notes (not re-checked after rewording).

evidence.text: On 27 May 2026 the Supreme Court upheld the ECI's power to conduct the SIR, including examining citizenship for inclusion on the rolls, and said it had not acted in excess of its statutory powers, with a presumption in favour of electors already on the rolls.

In October 2025 the ECI's counsel told the court that no deleted voter had filed an appeal or complaint with it; the court said it could not hold a roving inquiry and asked for affidavits from those aggrieved, while ADR said it could produce 100.
The Bihar Chief Electoral Officer's office attributed draft-stage deletions to deaths (about 22 lakh), migration or absence (about 36 lakh) and duplicates (about 7 lakh).

arguments.reasoning: The Supreme Court found the SIR lawful with safeguards, the state's election office gives deaths, migration and duplicates as the reasons, and the ECI said no deleted voter had appealed.
arguments.title: The court upheld it, and the ECI says no one appealed

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The Karnataka CID's SIT chargesheet names a former BJP MLA and his son as prime accused in an alleged conspiracy to file 5,994 fraudulent deletion applications between December 2022 and February 2023.

An ECI press release of 19 September 2025 said it received 6,018 online deletion applications for Aland, rejected 5,994 as incorrect and approved 24; the ECI filed a police complaint on 21 February 2023 after a complaint from MLA B R Patil.

arguments.reasoning: Police have charged named people for a paid scheme of fake deletion requests, and the ECI's figures show thousands of such requests.
arguments.title: A chargesheet and the ECI's own numbers

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: Reporting on the chargesheet says the CID wrote 18 letters asking the ECI for technical data and that the ECI did not share it.

arguments.reasoning: If the CID asked repeatedly for technical data and did not get it, the probe was held back.
arguments.title: Investigators say their requests went unanswered

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The ECI said the case was registered by its own authority in 2023 and that it handed over all available information to the Karnataka CID.

arguments.reasoning: The ECI itself registered the first complaint and says it handed over all available information, which does not fit a body holding back data.
arguments.title: The ECI says it gave everything and started the case

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed; the checker found the reasoning overreached, so it was reworded to its notes (not re-checked after rewording).

evidence.text: Rahul Gandhi said a Congress research team found over one lakh fake votes in Mahadevapura out of about 6.5 lakh, in four categories: fake names, duplicates, invalid addresses and bulk additions.
He said Maharashtra had 9.7 crore voters against an adult population of 9.54 crore, with about 39 lakh added between the 2024 Lok Sabha and assembly polls.

arguments.reasoning: If one seat has over a lakh suspect entries and, on Congress's figures, a state has more voters than its projected adult population, that suggests the rolls were padded.
arguments.title: The opposition's analysis of the rolls

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: EC sources said Maharashtra's electors rose 8.14% between the 2019 and 2024 assembly polls, less than Jharkhand (13.40%) or Telangana (16.16%) over their own cycles, and only 89 first appeals were filed after the rolls were finalised.

Karnataka's Chief Electoral Officer asked Rahul Gandhi to sign a declaration under Rule 20(3)(b) naming the electors, and the CEC said he must give an affidavit within seven days or apologise, failing which the allegations would be treated as baseless.

arguments.reasoning: On EC figures, Maharashtra's growth was lower than in some other states, few appeals were filed, and the claims have not been submitted in the sworn form that would let officials check each name.
arguments.title: The ECI's numbers, and no sworn complaint

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: ADR alleged tampering and data discrepancies and argued that VVPAT checks in only five randomly selected polling stations per constituency were insufficient.

arguments.reasoning: Petitioners alleged data discrepancies and argued that checking paper slips in only five polling stations per seat leaves tampering possible.
arguments.title: Checks are too thin to catch tampering

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: In April 2024 the Supreme Court rejected all pleas for 100% VVPAT verification, including the suggestion to return to paper ballots, and made no finding of tampering.
It ordered symbol loading units sealed for 45 days and allowed the second- or third-placed candidate to request a burnt-memory check of 5% of a seat's EVMs.

arguments.reasoning: After questioning the ECI at length on the machines, the court dismissed the pleas and added further checks; no tampering has been shown.
arguments.title: The Supreme Court examined it and made no finding of tampering

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: On complaints about the Prime Minister's April 2024 Banswara speech, the ECI sent its notice to BJP president J P Nadda; the letter did not name Modi.

arguments.reasoning: When the complaint was about the Prime Minister's own words, the ECI wrote to the BJP president instead, a softer step.
arguments.title: The PM's speech drew a notice to his party, not to him

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge received a similarly worded notice about complaints against him and Rahul Gandhi; the report says the Commission was holding party presidents responsible as a first step to rein in star campaigners.
Officials quoted in the report said it was the first time the Commission had taken cognisance of a complaint against any prime minister.

arguments.reasoning: The ECI handled complaints against Congress leaders the same way, through their party president, and it was the first time it took cognisance of a complaint against any prime minister.
arguments.title: Both parties got the same treatment

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: In December 2024 Rule 93(2)(a) was amended, on the ECI's recommendation, so that only papers specified in the rules are open to public inspection, after a High Court ordered footage and documents released to a non-candidate.

In June 2025 the ECI cut the retention of polling video and photos to 45 days, from three months to a year, citing misuse of clips by non-contestants; footage is kept longer where an election petition is filed, and 45 days matches the window for filing one.

arguments.reasoning: The rule on which election papers the public may inspect was narrowed, and footage is now kept for a shorter time unless an election petition is filed.
arguments.title: A narrowed rule and a shorter retention period

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The Indian Express reported that Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded objections at least 14 times over ten months, on voter additions and deletions, Form 6, and control of the roll database.
They recorded that some decisions were issued without their knowledge, and Sandhu called a Form 6 change "unauthorised and illegal".

arguments.reasoning: If two of three commissioners repeatedly object on record, and say some decisions were issued without their knowledge, the CEC is deciding over their objections.
arguments.title: Fourteen dissent notes on record

evidence.text: The ECI said differing views are a normal part of deliberation and that its decisions over the past year were unanimous; it did not dispute that the notes exist.

arguments.reasoning: Differing views are normal while deciding, and the ECI says the decisions themselves were taken unanimously.
arguments.title: The ECI says its decisions were unanimous

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed; the checker found the reasoning overreached, so it was reworded to its notes (not re-checked after rewording).

evidence.text: Removal notices against the CEC signed by 130 Lok Sabha and 63 Rajya Sabha MPs were declined in April 2026; the bulletins gave no specific reasons, though the Rajya Sabha Chairman was reported to have found no prima facie case of misbehaviour.
A 2023 paper by Sabyasachi Das, not peer reviewed at the time, found the BJP won a disproportionate share of close 2019 contests, concentrated in BJP-ruled states.

arguments.reasoning: The government side holds the majority in picking commissioners, the Commission's contested decisions are the subject of formal removal notices that were declined, and a study found close-seat anomalies favouring the ruling party; critics read these together as a shared aim, though none of them shows coordination directly.
arguments.title: The pieces point one way

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed; the checker found the reasoning overreached, so it was reworded to its notes (not re-checked after rewording).

evidence.text: In the 2024 Lok Sabha election the BJP won 240 seats, short of the 272 majority mark; the NDA won 293 and formed the government.
In May 2026 Vijay's TVK became the largest party in Tamil Nadu with 108 seats and the BJP won 1, and Congress won Kerala; in the same round the BJP swept West Bengal and retained Assam.

arguments.reasoning: If the referee and government were tilting elections together, the ruling party would be unlikely to lose its own majority in 2024 and lose states like Tamil Nadu and Kerala under the same Commission, even as it won others.
arguments.title: The ruling party still loses majorities and states

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The Supreme Court upheld the SIR as within the ECI's powers.
The Das paper states that it does not provide 'proofs of fraud'; Scroll describes it as a probabilistic exercise.

arguments.reasoning: Each decision has its own stated legal reason, the biggest one was upheld by the Supreme Court, and the study's author says it is not proof; a run of contested decisions does not show that two bodies agreed on an aim.
arguments.title: A pattern is not a plan

arguments.check_note: Cross-checked: evidence confirmed against its cited sources by an independent agent pass; where it suggested corrected wording, that wording was applied.

evidence.text: The Das paper's anomaly was specific to closely fought seats.

arguments.reasoning: Unfairness at the margins would show up in close seats, not in landslides, so big opposition wins do not show the process is fair.
arguments.title: Losing some races does not rule out tilting close ones

priorities.emphasised_by: critics of the 2023 law, echoed from the bench in July 2026
priorities.text: The referee must be seen to be independent, not only be independent.
An elected Parliament makes the law on appointments, and constitutional offices should not be presumed to act in bad faith.
Clean rolls: no dead, shifted, duplicate or ineligible names.
No eligible voter left off, and the burden of proof on the state rather than the voter.
Election records open enough that anyone can check them.
Voter privacy, and stopping selective clips being used to mislead.

priorities.emphasised_by: Justice Datta, in the 2024 VVPAT judgment
priorities.text: Trust in a working system, without unwarranted suspicion.

question.original: CEC and modi government, together are trying to rig Indian democracy
question.plain: Are the Chief Election Commissioner and the Union government working together to make India's elections unfair?
question.reframe_note: "Rig" is replaced with "make elections unfair" so the question reads the same to both sides. The claim is then split into parts that can each be checked: how the referee is appointed, what happened to voter rolls, voting machines, rule enforcement, transparency, how the Commission works inside, and finally intent.

evidence.text: The Supreme Court upheld the SIR as within the ECI's powers.

provenance.source_citation: Scroll, A new research paper argues manipulation in 2019 polls. What does this mean for the EC? (2023-08-14) https://scroll.in/article/1054262/a-new-research-paper-argues-manipulation-in-2019-polls-what-does-this-mean-for-the-ec

evidence.text: The Das paper's anomaly was specific to closely fought seats.

inferences.text: The government side holds the majority in picking commissioners, the Commission's contested decisions are the subject of formal removal notices that were declined, and a study found close-seat anomalies favouring the ruling party; critics read these together as a shared aim, though none of them shows coordination directly.

If the referee and government were tilting elections together, the ruling party would be unlikely to lose its own majority in 2024 and lose states like Tamil Nadu and Kerala under the same Commission, even as it won others.

Each decision has its own stated legal reason, the biggest one was upheld by the Supreme Court, and the study's author says it is not proof; a run of contested decisions does not show that two bodies agreed on an aim.
Unfairness at the margins would show up in close seats, not in landslides, so big opposition wins do not show the process is fair.

preferences.rationale: A Supreme Court bench questioned the ECI at length on the machines and safeguards and made no finding of tampering; the petition argued that checks were too few, which is a case for more checking, not evidence that tampering happened.
